content: A database search identified 183 citations and 243 conference abstracts. No additional studies were found through other methods. After removing duplicates, 392 records were reviewed. Of these, 131 article citations and 236 abstracts were excluded for being unrelated to the study topic. Following a detailed review by two independent screeners, 17 articles and 7 abstracts remained. However, 16 articles were excluded for not meeting the study design criteria and were categorized as background or values and preferences. Additionally, 6 abstracts were excluded as they provided supplementary information on the included trial but did not report key outcomes. Ultimately, one study, with data reported in one article and one conference abstract, was deemed eligible for inclusion in the review. The included study was a randomized controlled trial conducted in Bangkok, Thailand, to evaluate whether daily oral use of tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (tenofovir) could reduce HIV transmission among injecting drug users. A total of 2,413 participants were recruited from 17 drug treatment clinics. Of these participants, 80% were male, and 63% reported injecting drugs in the past 12 weeks. The study was assessed using the Cochrane Risk of Bias tool and was judged to have a low risk of bias across the following categories: random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding of participants and personnel, blinding of outcome assessment, and selective reporting. Initially, the study was judged to have an uncertain risk of bias for selective reporting. However, the study protocol was available, and all pre-specified primary outcomes were reported as planned. Data on two secondary outcomes, condom use and the number of sexual partners, were not available in the pre-specified format in published reports. After contacting the study authors, additional unpublished data were provided, leading to a revised judgment of low risk for selective reporting. For incomplete outcome data (attrition bias), the study noted a high loss to follow-up relative to the number of events. This included 6% loss in the placebo group, with additional participants from both groups withdrawing, dying, or otherwise stopping follow-up. As a result, the study was judged to have a high risk of bias for this measure, and the quality of evidence was downgraded due to the potential risk of bias across all study outcomes. This was particularly significant as the single trial was the only source of evidence for all outcomes. The study measured seven key outcomes: (1) HIV infection, (2) any adverse event, (3) any stage 3 or 4 adverse event, (4) condom use, (5) number of sexual partners, (6) injection frequency, and (7) needle/syringe sharing. Results for each outcome are as follows: 1. HIV Infection: The incidence of HIV infection was significantly reduced among participants in the tenofovir arm compared to the control arm, based on both intention-to-treat and modified intention-to-treat analyses. Age-stratified analyses showed that pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) was effective in participants aged 40 and older, while no significant difference was observed in the 20–29 and 30–39 age groups, although results trended positively. 2. Adverse Events: There was no statistically significant difference in reported adverse events between the two study arms. In the tenofovir arm, 91% of participants experienced an adverse event, compared to 90% in the placebo arm. 3. Stage 3 or 4 Adverse Events: Both study arms reported similar rates of stage 3 and 4 adverse events. In the tenofovir arm, 13% of participants experienced such events, compared to 13% in the placebo arm. 4. Condom Use: Data on condom use were not reported in published articles or abstracts at the time of the search. However, additional unpublished data provided by the study authors indicated that 5% of tenofovir arm participants with live-in partners reported always using condoms, compared to 5% in the placebo arm. A skip pattern error in the initial years of the study rendered data on condom use with casual partners unreliable. 5. Number of Sexual Partners: Self-reported data on having more than one sexual partner in the previous three months decreased from 22% at enrollment to 11% at 12 months and 6% at 72 months across both study arms. Regression analyses showed no interaction between time and treatment group for this outcome. 6. Injection Frequency: Self-reported injection drug use in the previous three months decreased from 63% at enrollment to 23% at 12 months and 18% at 72 months across both study arms. Regression analyses showed no interaction between time and treatment group for this outcome. 7. Needle/Syringe Sharing: Self-reported needle sharing in the previous three months decreased from 18% at enrollment to 2% at 12 months and 1% at 72 months across both study arms. Regression analyses showed no interaction between time and treatment group for this outcome. The study also explored values and preferences regarding PrEP among people who inject drugs (PWID). A systematic review identified one study examining the acceptability of PrEP among PWID in Ukraine. Most participants expressed willingness to use PrEP if it became available, even when considering potential side effects, the need for condom use, and regular HIV testing. Route of administration was identified as the most important factor influencing PrEP uptake, with injections preferred over daily or coitally-dependent pills. Concerns about stigma, criminalization, and feasibility were noted, particularly in settings where injection drug use is illegal. In summary, the Bangkok Tenofovir Study demonstrated that daily oral tenofovir significantly reduced HIV transmission among injecting drug users, with no significant differences in adverse events between study arms. However, high loss to follow-up and reliance on a single trial limited the overall quality of evidence.
